## Overview

In class, we started from a default chart and asked one question about every change: **what does this choice make the reader see?**

This week you'll make those decisions yourself, on new data: visits to the U.S. National Parks, from the National Park Service, as collected for TidyTuesday. Kentucky has one of the parks in the data: Mammoth Cave.

The question: **Where does Mammoth Cave sit among the National Parks?**

This weekly is about **visualization judgment**. You'll do a little cleaning to get there, but the point is the charts and your reasons for them.

A few things:

# Part 1: Get the data, and know what you're plotting

The data is here:

`https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/master/data/2019/2019-09-17/national_parks.csv`

Read it in and save a copy to `data/raw/national_parks.csv`. Then read your saved copy and call it `parks_raw`.

WAS HAVING PROBLEMS WITH IT NOT FINDING MY DATA/RAW FOLDER HAD TO USE AI TO FIGURE IT OUT. THAT IS WHERE THE DIR.CREATE CAME FROM

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| eval: false

library(tidyverse)

 dir.create("data/raw", recursive = TRUE)
 parks_raw <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/master/data/2019/2019-09-17/national_parks.csv")
 write_csv(parks_raw,"data/raw/national_parks.csv")

```

```{r}
#| warning: false

parks_raw <- read_csv("data/raw/national_parks.csv")

```

> What type is `year`? Why isn't it numeric?

As you scroll to the bottom the numeric year such as 1973 changes to Total for some reason. Total cannot be a value.

```{r}
#| warning: false

view(parks_raw)

```

> Why would leaving the `Total` rows in create a problem for an analysis of annual visitation?
>
> If you were trying to get a sum of just the years, if you throw in a bunch of rows of cumulative annual visitation, it would screw up the results.

> How many kinds of `unit_type` are there?
>
> There are 30 different types of unit_type. I know this because there are 30 rows
>
> For this assignment, keep only `National Park` records and annual observations. Call the result `np`, and make `year` a number.

```{r}
#| warning: false

parks_raw |> 
  count(unit_type)

np <- parks_raw |> 
  filter(unit_type == "National Park", year != "Total") |> 
  mutate(year = as.numeric(year))
```

> Before we visualize anything, check whether one row is one park in one year.

```{r}
#| warning: false

np |> 
  count(unit_code, year) |> 
  filter(n == 2)



```

You should find one park that appears twice in the same year. Here's the cleaning decision for it; run this:

```{r}
#| warning: false

np <- np |>
  distinct(unit_code, year, .keep_all = TRUE)
```

> After that cleaning, what does one row represent?
>
> One row represents the total number of visitors for one year at a specific national park
>
> How many parks are represented?
>
> There are 60 parks represented.
>
> What years does the file cover?
>
> The file covers years from 1904 - 2016

```{r}
#| warning: false

view(np)
np |> 
  summarise(
    n_distinct(unit_code),
    min(year),
    max(year)
  )
  

```

> Why does the ending year matter for the claims you make later?
>
> It does not contain data up to the current year 2026.

# Part 2: Start with the obvious chart

Your audience wants to know how the National Parks compared in 2016.

```{r}
#| warning: false

parks_2016 <- np |>
  filter(year == 2016)
```

> Make the most obvious bar chart: park on the x-axis and 2016 visitors on the y-axis. Don't improve it yet.

```{r}
#| warning: false
view(parks_2016)
 ggplot(parks_2016, aes(x = parkname, y = visitors)) +
   geom_col()

```

> Is the chart technically correct? What makes it difficult to use?
>
> The chart is technically right, but it is impossible to use because the park names are so condensed that you cant even read them. and visitors values is in scientific notation.

# Part 3: Make the comparison readable

> Revise the chart so the park names are readable and the ordering helps the reader compare visitation.

```{r}
#| warning: false

ggplot(parks_2016, aes(x = visitors, y = fct_reorder(parkname, visitors))) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma)
 

```

> Why put park names on the y-axis instead of the x-axis?
>
> Putting the park names on the Y axis makes it easier to view the names because there are less names than visitors so they are easier to see when they are not overlapping.

> Why reorder the parks by visitors?
>
> It is easier to compare the bar chart when the values are side by side, it is easily visible to see which park has more or less than another. It also makes it easier to see when they are compared by value and not by names.

> Should every park get its own color?
>
> No because it would look like a mess and it doesn't really add anything to add color to each value.

# Part 4: A real visualization problem

Mammoth Cave is the local park we care about. First, find where it ranks in 2016.

Mammoth ranks 33rd in visitation

```{r}
#| warning: false

parks_2016 |> 
  arrange(desc(visitors))

```

Now the design problem:

> A chart of only the top 10 parks makes Mammoth Cave disappear. A chart with 60 equally emphasized parks makes the reader work too hard. Create one visualization that helps a reader understand where Mammoth Cave sits relative to the other National Parks.

There is no one right chart here. Make the one you can defend.

```{r}
#| warning: false

top_parks_2016 <- parks_2016 |> 
  slice_max(visitors, n = 35)

ggplot(top_parks_2016, aes(x = visitors, y = fct_reorder(parkname, visitors), fill = (parkname == "Mammoth Cave"))) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "red", "FALSE" = "grey"))
  




```

# Part 5: Defend the choices

> What should the reader notice first when they look at your final chart?
>
> The reader should first notice that the mammoth cave bar is a significantly different color than the other national parks. The mammoth cave bar is red while the others are grey.

> Name two visualization choices you made deliberately. For each one, explain what that choice helps the reader see.
>
> I actually like the bar chart I think it works it just needed some adjustments. I reduced the amount of national parks that had considerably less visitation than mammoth cave which makes the y axis easier to read because there is less cramming. I also made the value of mammoth cave red while the rest of the chart values are grey. It makes it instantly noticeable and easy to read.

> Name one visualization choice you considered but rejected. Why did you reject it?
>
> I first attempted a scatterplot and I thought it looked pretty stupid. Although i think I did something wrong because it came out looking like a bar chart with dots.

> What does your chart support saying? What does it **not** support saying?
>
> My chart can firmly say mammoth cave sits in the top 35 of national parks, it does not support how it ranks in other years because it is just 2016

# Bringing it together

> In 3–4 sentences, answer the question for your reader: where does Mammoth Cave sit among the National Parks? Include one number, one interpretation, and one limitation.
>
> Mammoth cave sits at the 33rd most visited National park. It is a middle of the pack park in terms of visitation. It is nowhere near close to the most visited held by the grand canyon, but it sees significantly more visitation than the gates of the arctic. However this data is just for 2016.
